name: Shang dynasty (Wu Ding)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes Late Shang Polity Territory at 1,000,000 km2; Taagepera 1978 gives 1.25 million km2 at 1122 BCE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires). Low = a royal domain plus close allies only (educated guess). Border = historical-basemaps world_bc1500 polygon 'Zhoa' (sic), which contains Anyang and Zhengzhou and measures ~1,170,000 km2 computed from the GeoJSON, consistent with the Seshat/Taagepera sphere of influence rather than direct rule.

population.note: Seshat codes Late Shang (1250-1045 BCE) population at 5,000,000 (single value). OWID/HYDE (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) gives 12.9 M for all of present-day China in 2000 and 1000 BCE, an upper envelope. Range is wide because Shang direct control vs allied fang states is unclear.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Yinxu was a large dispersed settlement (Seshat codes the largest settlement at only 4,000, which reflects one ward); most people lived in villages.

activePersonnel.note: Sawyer and Sawyer 1994 (pp. 33-34, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty): the Shang king kept about 1,000 troops at the capital; oracle-bone inscriptions show musters of 3,000-5,000 for border campaigns and up to 13,000 for suppressing rebellions (Wu Ding era; Fu Hao led such levies). From Wu Ding on, standing warriors increased and commoners (zhongren) were conscripted (Sawyer 2011 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Shang_dynasty). The Shiji's 700,000 Shang troops at Muye (1046 BCE) are rejected. Mid = royal troops, lineage forces and one rebellion-scale muster plus border garrisons.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Commoner (zhongren) levies of royal and lineage estates.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Chariot crews (3 per vehicle), dog and horse officers, supply carriers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Lineage armies plus conscripted commoners; the 13,000 musters suggest a low share of the population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Sawyer and Sawyer 1994 (pp. 33-34, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty): the Shang king kept about 1,000 troops at the capital; oracle-bone inscriptions show musters of 3,000-5,000 for border campaigns and up to 13,000 for suppressing rebellions (Wu Ding era; Fu Hao led such levies). From Wu Ding on, standing warriors increased and commoners (zhongren) were conscripted (Sawyer 2011 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Shang_dynasty). The Shiji's 700,000 Shang troops at Muye (1046 BCE) are rejected. Split: dagger-axe and spear infantry ~60%.

quality.note: Bronze dagger-axes (ge), spears, bronze or leather helmets; stone weapons still in use by commoners.

count.note: Sawyer and Sawyer 1994 (pp. 33-34, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty): the Shang king kept about 1,000 troops at the capital; oracle-bone inscriptions show musters of 3,000-5,000 for border campaigns and up to 13,000 for suppressing rebellions (Wu Ding era; Fu Hao led such levies). From Wu Ding on, standing warriors increased and commoners (zhongren) were conscripted (Sawyer 2011 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Shang_dynasty). The Shiji's 700,000 Shang troops at Muye (1046 BCE) are rejected. Split: archers ~27% ('Many Archers' office; officials trained archery).

quality.note: Reflex bows of 60-70 m effective range (Shaughnessy via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Shang_dynasty); bone arrowheads outnumber bronze 20 to 1.

count.note: Sawyer and Sawyer 1994 (pp. 33-34, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty): the Shang king kept about 1,000 troops at the capital; oracle-bone inscriptions show musters of 3,000-5,000 for border campaigns and up to 13,000 for suppressing rebellions (Wu Ding era; Fu Hao led such levies). From Wu Ding on, standing warriors increased and commoners (zhongren) were conscripted (Sawyer 2011 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Shang_dynasty). The Shiji's 700,000 Shang troops at Muye (1046 BCE) are rejected. Split: skirmishers and allied Yi archers ~13%.

Chariots reached Shang China c. 1200 BCE from the northern steppe (Wu 2013, Rawson 2020 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty); under the Shang they were ornate command and archery platforms with a chariot-to-foot ratio of about 1:30 (Lee 2016 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Shang_dynasty), so a 13,000 muster implies at most ~400. At 1250 the chariot was just arriving, so mid is low. Crews in supportPersonnel.

quality.note: Ornate, heavy-wheeled early chariots; few and used mainly by commanders.

training.note: Aristocratic crews new to the weapon.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5: king as commander, defined posts (ma, ya, she, shu), divination-driven decisions, left/centre/right formations, ambush and reconnaissance in use.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: clan-based armies, unstable allied fang states.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5: Wu Ding's long successful campaigns against the Guifang, Tufang and Qiang.

weapons.note: Between anchors 1 and 2: bronze dagger-axe, reflex bow; the war chariot just arriving.

armor.note: Between 1 and 2: leather armour and shields, bronze helmets for elites.

fortification.note: Between 1 and 2: rammed-earth city walls (Zhengzhou, Yanshi); Yinxu itself unwalled.

logistics.note: Between 1 and 2: state granaries, carriers, river transport.

communications.note: Between 1 and 2: reporting network of boats, chariots, runners and drums (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Shang_dynasty).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: China 1000 CE = 1,225 (2011 int$), the earliest Chinese value; Bronze Age millet agriculture with stone and wooden tools scaled down by ~40%.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Royal bronze foundries produced weapons and chariot fittings; frequent campaigns.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Large bronze, bone and jade workshops at Yinxu; agrarian base.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Millet and wheat farming on the North China loess plain.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; Bronze Age life expectancy was if anything lower, so this is not an underestimate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. No engineered road system attested.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Short-range campaigns from the capital region.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Oxen, pigs used for transport little; horses rare until the chariot.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1: home plain, local supply; capital unwalled.

notes: Snapshot = c. 1250 BCE, Wu Ding's reign at Yinxu. The chariot-archetype doctrine overstates Shang chariot use: infantry with dagger-axes and bows dominated and chariots were few elite platforms. Army sizes come from oracle-bone muster figures as summarised by Sawyer; traditional texts (Shiji: 700,000 at Muye) are rejected. Border polygon is a sphere-of-influence approximation; population convention: everything inside it per Seshat's 5 M.
